prompt.context: Your client is a clothing retailer similar to the Gap or Abercrombie & Fitch. They have expanded their number of store locations and achieved significant sales growth. As a result, they are considering an IPO. However, recently the company had moved from profits to losses.
prompt.question: The CEO needs to understand why the company has moved from profits to losses, and what needs to be done to become profitable again.

clarifying_info.q: How has revenue trended over time?
clarifying_info.a: The interviewer shows the Revenue Growth graph (Exhibit 1): revenues grew from $0.2M in 1990 to $28M in 1998.

clarifying_info.q: How has the number of store locations changed?
clarifying_info.a: The interviewer shows the Store Locations graph (Exhibit 2): the company had 1 store from 1990-1993, added 2 more in 1994 (total 3), kept 3 in 1995, jumped to 10 in 1996, then 40 in 1997, and remained at 40 in 1998.
Fixed costs are $1 million per location per year (lease, utilities, store manager, etc.). Variable costs equal 20% of sales (cost of clothing, sales people, etc.). Corporate overhead is minimal.

exhibits.title: Revenue Growth
exhibits.shows: A bar chart of annual revenue (in millions $) from 1990 to 1998

exhibits.title: Number of Store Locations
exhibits.shows: A bar chart of the total number of store locations from 1990 to 1998

framework: Diagnose the profitability problem: Revenue vs. Cost structure
Examine revenue growth relative to store expansion
Analyze per-store economics: fixed cost per location vs. variable cost vs. revenue per store
Identify the store lifecycle effect: new stores ramp up sales over time
Quantify the profitability gap caused by rapid store openings
Develop recommendations to restore profitability for an IPO

questions.prompt: Using the exhibits and cost data provided, determine why the company moved from profits to losses.
questions.guidance: The key insight is that the single original store grew revenue significantly over time, indicating stores require a ramp-up period before becoming profitable. With rapid expansion (1 store to 40 stores between 1993 and 1997), most stores are newly opened and in the loss-making early phase of their lifecycle, dragging aggregate results into the red.

math.setup: Check profitability of the original store in 1993 (when there was still only 1 store). Revenue in 1993 = $2M. Fixed cost = $1M. Variable cost = 20% of $2M = $0.4M. Profit = Revenue - Fixed cost - Variable cost.
steps: So in 1993 the single store earned $0.6M profit
math.answer: The original store was profitable by 1993 with $0.6M profit. Subsequent new stores need similar time to ramp. By 1997-1998, 37-39 of the 40 stores are newly opened and likely generating losses, explaining the aggregate swing to losses.

questions.prompt: Estimate total company profitability in 1998 to illustrate the problem quantitatively.
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply per-store economics at the aggregate level. With $28M total revenue across 40 stores, average revenue per store is $0.7M, well below the $1.25M break-even point. Total fixed costs alone are $40M, far exceeding contribution margin.

math.setup: Total revenue 1998 = $28M across 40 stores. Fixed cost = $1M * 40 stores = $40M. Variable cost = 20% * $28M = $5.6M. Profit = Revenue - Fixed - Variable.
steps: Break-even revenue per store = $1M / 0.80 = $1.25M; average actual = $28M / 40 = $0.7M per store
math.answer: The company loses approximately $17.6M in 1998. Average store revenue ($0.7M) is far below the break-even threshold ($1.25M), driven by the large cohort of recently opened stores.

brainstorming.prompt: What recommendations would you make to the CEO?

categories.name: IPO readiness
ideas: Slow the rate of new store openings so a larger share of stores are in the profitable portion of their lifecycle
Delay IPO until aggregate profitability is demonstrated

categories.name: Operational reporting
ideas: Develop per-location P&L reporting so management can track individual store profitability rather than only aggregate results
Create a store lifecycle model showing expected revenue ramp-up at each stage

categories.name: Performance management
ideas: Benchmark successful mature locations to establish realistic revenue targets at each lifecycle stage
Set hurdle rates for new stores; close locations that fail to hit targets within a defined period
Identify best-performing stores and replicate their practices across the portfolio

recommendation: Slow the pace of new store openings to allow the existing portfolio to mature and reach profitability before opening additional locations
Implement per-store profitability reporting and a store lifecycle model to give management visibility into individual location performance
risks: Slowing expansion may signal weakness to potential IPO investors if not communicated as a deliberate strategy
Some recently opened stores may never reach adequate performance in their current locations and could require closure
next_steps: Build a detailed store-level profitability model segmented by store age/cohort
Establish hurdle metrics for new stores based on the performance trajectory of mature locations
Define a revised IPO timeline contingent on achieving target aggregate profitability
